text: Every pool in Lessons 5 through 8 spread an LP's capital across the entire price curve, from zero to infinity. Most of that capital sits at prices that will realistically never be reached — earning zero fees while still counting as deposited. Concentrated liquidity exists to fix exactly that.

Instead of spreading liquidity across the whole curve, an LP picks a price range and deposits only inside it. Full-range liquidity stretches from zero to infinity, with most of it never touched. Concentrated liquidity, say $1,800 to $2,200 around a $2,000 price, puts all of it where trading actually happens.

The efficiency gain is dramatic. A full-range LP typically has only one to two percent of their capital active near the current price at any moment. A concentrated LP depositing the same dollar amount inside a tight range can match that same fee-earning depth using roughly ten to twenty times less total capital.

This works through ticks — discrete price boundaries that define each position's edges. A position's liquidity only counts toward swap pricing, called active liquidity, while the current price sits between its lower and upper tick. Multiple LPs can stack overlapping ranges, and the pool's total active liquidity is just the sum of everyone whose range contains that price.

Concentrated liquidity doesn't eliminate impermanent loss — it concentrates that exposure too. And it adds a new risk: if price moves outside your range, your position converts entirely into whichever asset is now cheaper, and you earn zero trading fees until price re-enters. A full-range position never runs out of range; it just always earns less efficiently.

Full-range is deposit-and-forget but inefficient. Concentrated is efficient but demands active management. Next: how overcollateralized lending turns a deposited asset into borrowing power, the mechanics behind protocols like Aave and Compound.
